parentTitle: The Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer Care
title: Person-centred dementia care
blurb: Coordinate person-centred dementia care, respond to distress by finding its cause, and know NICE NG97's limits on antipsychotics and other medicines.
question: Mrs Evans, 86, has Alzheimer's disease and lives in a care home. For four afternoons she has shouted, paced and pushed staff away during personal care. A carer asks whether the GP could prescribe something to calm her. What should the nurse do first?

teach.body: Dementia is a progressive condition in which memory, thinking, communication and daily functioning decline over months and years, unlike the sudden change of delirium. NICE NG97 builds care around the person: a single named professional coordinates care, plans are agreed with the person and family, and distress is treated as a message to understand, not a behaviour to sedate. Plain English: know the person (history, routines, what calms and upsets them) and you will often prevent the crisis. Tools such as 'This is Me' help share that knowledge.
teach.cite: NICE NG97 recs 1.3.1–1.3.2; 'This is Me' (Alzheimer's Society/RCN)

items: Arrange an initial needs assessment, face to face if possible.
Give information about services and how to access them.
Involve family or carers in support and decisions, as appropriate.
Give special consideration to the views of people who lack capacity (MCA principles), and tell them about advocacy, including an IMCA where relevant.
Develop a care and support plan: agreed with the person, covering comorbidities, stating when it will be reviewed, with a copy for the person and family.

teach.caption: NG97 recs 1.5.2–1.5.5 (Alzheimer's), 1.5.10 (Lewy bodies) and 1.5.15 (frontotemporal). Minimise medicines with anticholinergic burden at reviews (1.6.2).

steps.label: Structured assessment
steps.sub: Look for pain, delirium, inappropriate care

steps.label: Antipsychotic?
steps.sub: Risk of harm, or severe distress from agitation, hallucinations, delusions

steps.label: Reassess every 6 weeks
steps.sub: Stop if no clear ongoing benefit

teach.text: Do not confuse the reviews: antipsychotics in DEMENTIA are reassessed at least every 6 weeks (NG97), while haloperidol for DELIRIUM is short term, usually 1 week or less (CG103). In dementia with Lewy bodies or Parkinson's disease dementia, antipsychotics can cause severe sensitivity reactions. And no valproate for agitation unless indicated for another condition.

teach.caption: People with dementia are at increased risk of delirium in hospital (NG97 1.9.1). If unsure, manage delirium first (CG103 1.6.3).

teach.body: People with moderate to severe dementia may not be able to tell you they are in pain, so distress, resisting care or calling out may be pain. NICE suggests a structured observational pain assessment tool (such as Abbey or PAINAD) alongside self-report and standard clinical assessment in moderate to severe dementia, and alongside clinical assessment for people who cannot self-report. Repeat the assessment if they seem to be in pain, if behaviour changes, and after any pain intervention.

teach.h: Scenario: Mrs Evans in the care home
teach.body: Mrs Evans, 86, has Alzheimer's disease. For four afternoons she has shouted, paced and pushed staff away during personal care. Instead of asking for a sedative, the nurse does a structured assessment: her PAINAD score is raised when she moves her left knee, she has not opened her bowels for 5 days, and her 'This is Me' shows she always bathed in the morning. The team gives regular analgesia, treats the constipation, moves personal care to the morning and reassesses pain afterwards. The distress settles.

head: Do
Don't
rows: Group cognitive stimulation therapy (mild to moderate)
Acupuncture, ginseng, vitamin E to treat dementia
Psychological therapy for mild to moderate depression
Routine antidepressants for mild to moderate depression
Personalised sleep plan: daylight, exercise, activity
Melatonin for insomnia in Alzheimer's disease
Eye test after diagnosis, then every 2 years
Valproate for agitation (unless otherwise indicated)
teach.caption: NG97 recs 1.4.2, 1.4.5–1.4.6, 1.7.10–1.7.14, 1.8.11.

items: A single named professional coordinates care and agrees a reviewed care and support plan.
Distress: structured assessment first for pain, delirium or inappropriate care; psychosocial measures first-line.
Antipsychotics only for risk of harm or severe distress; lowest dose, shortest time, reassess at least every 6 weeks; caution in Lewy body and Parkinson's dementia.
No AChE inhibitors or memantine for frontotemporal dementia; do not stop AChE inhibitors for severity alone.
Use observational pain tools when self-report is unreliable, and repeat after treatment.

summary: You can now coordinate person-centred dementia care and respond to distress by looking for pain, delirium and care-related causes before medicines. You can also apply NICE NG97's rules on antipsychotics, dementia medicines, pain assessment and sleep.

A.q: Mr Shah, 80, has vascular dementia and lives in a care home. Over the past week he has started hitting out when staff help him wash in the morning. Before any treatment for his distress, what does NICE NG97 ask staff to do?
options: Ask the GP for a low-dose antipsychotic
Assess for causes such as pain, delirium or how care is given
Arrange a referral to the memory clinic for review
Increase staff numbers so that his personal care is completed quickly
A.why: NG97 rec 1.7.1: before starting non-drug or drug treatment for distress, do a structured assessment to explore reasons and check for clinical or environmental causes such as pain, delirium or inappropriate care.

whyNot.0: Antipsychotics are not first-line and come after assessment and psychosocial approaches, for specific indications.
whyNot.2: A referral does not replace assessing the immediate causes of his distress.
whyNot.3: More staff completing care quickly may itself be inappropriate care; the cause needs assessing first.

A.q: Mrs Cole, 84, has Alzheimer's disease and has been started on risperidone for distressing hallucinations. How often does NICE NG97 say she should be reassessed to check she still needs it?
options: At least every 2 weeks
At least every 12 weeks
At least every 6 weeks
At least every 6 months
A.why: NG97 rec 1.7.6: when using antipsychotics, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time and reassess at least every 6 weeks.

whyNot.0: NICE sets at least every 6 weeks, not every 2 weeks.
whyNot.1: 12 weeks is longer than the NICE maximum interval.
whyNot.3: 6 months is far longer than the NICE maximum interval.

A.q: Mr King, 62, has frontotemporal dementia. His daughter has read about donepezil and asks whether he could take it. What does NICE NG97 say?
options: It is offered as first-line for frontotemporal dementia
It is offered once the disease becomes severe
It is offered with memantine from diagnosis
It is not offered for frontotemporal dementia
A.why: NG97: do not offer AChE inhibitors (such as donepezil) or memantine to people with frontotemporal dementia.

whyNot.0: AChE inhibitors are options for mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease, not frontotemporal dementia.
whyNot.1: Severity does not change the advice for frontotemporal dementia.
whyNot.2: Neither donepezil nor memantine is offered for frontotemporal dementia.

B.q: Mrs Hill, 90, has severe dementia and cannot describe pain. She grimaces and calls out when she is turned. Which approach to assessing her pain does NICE NG97 suggest?
options: A structured observational pain tool such as PAINAD
A numerical pain rating scale from 0 to 10, asked twice daily
A pain diary completed by Mrs Hill
The Clinical Frailty Scale on admission
B.why: NG97 rec 1.8.3: consider a structured observational pain assessment tool alongside standard clinical assessment for people living with dementia who cannot self-report pain.

whyNot.1: A numerical scale relies on self-report, which she cannot give.
whyNot.2: A self-completed diary also relies on self-report.
whyNot.3: The Clinical Frailty Scale grades frailty, not pain.

B.q: Mrs Jones, 79, has Alzheimer's disease and wakes for long periods at night. Her GP suggests melatonin. Which response follows NICE NG97?
options: Give melatonin nightly and review it in 4 weeks
Query melatonin and suggest a personalised sleep plan
Suggest a sedating antihistamine at night instead of melatonin
Keep her in bed for longer each morning to rest
B.why: NG97 recs 1.7.13–1.7.14: do not offer melatonin for insomnia in Alzheimer's disease; consider a personalised multicomponent sleep approach (sleep hygiene, daylight, exercise, activities).

whyNot.0: NICE advises against melatonin for insomnia in Alzheimer's disease.
whyNot.2: Sedating antihistamines add anticholinergic burden, which NG97 asks teams to minimise.
whyNot.3: Extra time in bed works against the daylight, exercise and activity parts of a sleep plan.

B.q: Mr Fry, 90, has severe dementia and lives at home with carers. He has a chest infection that his GP believes can be treated at home. When deciding about hospital admission, what does NICE NG97 ask the team to weigh up?
options: His medical needs against harms such as delirium and disorientation
His bed availability today against the ward's current workload
His need for a full dementia reassessment while in hospital
His carers' preference for a respite break against the severity of his infection
B.why: NG97 rec 1.9.2: for a person with severe dementia, balance current medical needs against additional harms of hospital, such as disorientation, longer stay, mortality, delirium and an institutional environment.

whyNot.1: Bed availability is not the NICE balance; the person's needs and harms are.
whyNot.2: Admission is not recommended for dementia reassessment; NICE focuses on medical need against harm.
whyNot.3: Carers' needs matter, but NICE's balance is between his medical needs and the harms of admission.

C.q: Mr Lane, 79, has dementia with Lewy bodies and frightening visual hallucinations. The out-of-hours doctor plans to start haloperidol. What is the nurse's most important concern to raise?
options: A higher starting dose may be needed to settle him more quickly
Antipsychotics are first-line for Lewy body dementia
Valproate would be a safer choice for his symptoms
Antipsychotics can cause severe sensitivity reactions in him
C.why: NG97 rec 1.7.4: in dementia with Lewy bodies or Parkinson's disease dementia, antipsychotics can worsen motor features and cause severe antipsychotic sensitivity reactions.

whyNot.0: NICE asks for the lowest effective dose; a higher dose increases the risk.
whyNot.1: Antipsychotics are not first-line, and Lewy body dementia makes them riskier.
whyNot.2: NG97 rec 1.7.10: do not offer valproate for agitation or aggression in dementia unless indicated for another condition.

C.q: Mrs Patel, 85, has Alzheimer's disease that has progressed from moderate to severe. She has taken donepezil for 3 years and tolerates it. A locum suggests stopping it because her dementia is now severe. What does NICE NG97 advise?
options: Stop donepezil, as it does not work in severe disease
Switch donepezil to memantine monotherapy
Continue donepezil and offer memantine in addition
Continue donepezil and make no other change
C.why: NG97 rec 1.5.4: offer memantine in addition to an AChE inhibitor in severe Alzheimer's disease; rec 1.5.5: do not stop AChE inhibitors because of disease severity alone.

whyNot.0: NICE says do not stop AChE inhibitors because of disease severity alone.
whyNot.1: Memantine monotherapy is for those intolerant of AChE inhibitors or not taking one; she tolerates donepezil.
whyNot.3: In severe disease NICE says offer memantine in addition, so no change misses that.

C.q: Mr Okafor, 79, has mixed dementia and has just been allocated a named care coordinator. Which task is part of that coordinator's role in NICE NG97?
options: Making decisions for him whenever he lacks capacity
Prescribing and reviewing all of his dementia medicines
Replacing his GP for the management of all his other conditions
Agreeing a care plan that states when it will be reviewed
C.why: NG97 rec 1.3.2: named professionals develop a care and support plan, agree and review it with the person and family, specify when and how often it will be reviewed, and give them a copy.

whyNot.0: The coordinator gives special consideration to his views under the MCA; it does not make them his decision-maker.
whyNot.1: Prescribing follows NG97 1.5.5 by suitable clinicians; it is not the coordinator role.
whyNot.2: The plan covers comorbidities, but the coordinator does not replace his GP.

reteach.title: Distress is communication
reteach.question: When a person with dementia shouts or pushes staff away, what is the first question to ask?

blocks.h: Ask 'what is causing this?' before 'what will calm this?'
blocks.body: Many people with dementia cannot say 'my knee hurts', 'I am constipated', 'I feel ill' or 'you are rushing me'. Behaviour becomes the message. NICE NG97 puts a structured assessment for causes such as pain, delirium and inappropriate care first, then psychosocial and environmental changes. Antipsychotics are kept for risk of harm or severe distress, at the lowest dose for the shortest time.

blocks.text: Six weeks: the maximum interval between antipsychotic reassessments in dementia. Stop if there is no clear ongoing benefit.

explain.body: Each person living with dementia should have a single named health or social care professional coordinating care, with a care and support plan agreed with the person and family, reviewed at set times and shared between settings with consent. Life-story tools such as 'This is Me' help staff know the person.

test.q: Mr Ali, 82, has dementia and sees a memory clinic, a district nurse, a social worker and his GP. What does NICE NG97 say he should have?
options: A separate care plan from each of the four services
A single named professional coordinating his care
A case review by his GP once he loses capacity
A care home placement to bring services together
test.why: NG97 rec 1.3.1: provide people living with dementia with a single named health or social care professional responsible for coordinating their care.

whyNot.0: Separate plans fragment care; NICE asks for one coordinator and a shared plan.
whyNot.2: Coordination is needed from diagnosis, not once capacity is lost.
whyNot.3: A placement is not the NICE answer to coordinating community services.

explain.body: AChE inhibitors (donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine) for mild to moderate Alzheimer's; memantine for moderate disease if AChE inhibitors are unsuitable, or severe disease; donepezil or rivastigmine for Lewy body dementia; none for frontotemporal dementia. Minimise anticholinergic burden.

test.q: Mrs Grey, 76, is newly diagnosed with mild Alzheimer's disease. Which medicine option does NICE NG97 recommend?
options: Memantine monotherapy from diagnosis
An AChE inhibitor such as donepezil
Low-dose risperidone at night
Vitamin E supplements daily
test.why: NG97 rec 1.5.2: the AChE inhibitors donepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine are options for mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease.

whyNot.0: Memantine monotherapy is for moderate disease when AChE inhibitors are unsuitable, or for severe disease.
whyNot.2: Antipsychotics treat severe distress or risk of harm, not the dementia itself.
whyNot.3: NG97 rec 1.4.6: do not offer vitamin E to treat dementia.

explain.body: Offer only when the person is at risk of harming themselves or others, or has agitation, hallucinations or delusions causing severe distress. Discuss benefits and harms first; lowest effective dose, shortest time; reassess at least every 6 weeks; stop if no clear ongoing benefit.

test.q: In which situation does NICE NG97 allow an antipsychotic to be offered to a person with dementia?
options: Repeated questions that frustrate family carers
Wandering at night without distress or risk
Delusions that are causing severe distress
Refusing meals during a busy lunchtime
test.why: NG97 rec 1.7.3: offer antipsychotics only if the person is at risk of harming themselves or others, or has agitation, hallucinations or delusions causing severe distress.

whyNot.0: Repetitive questioning is not a NICE indication; it calls for psychosocial support.
whyNot.1: Wandering without distress or risk does not meet the criteria.
whyNot.3: Meal refusal needs assessment for causes, not an antipsychotic.

explain.body: Use a structured observational pain tool when the person cannot self-report, and repeat assessments after any intervention and when behaviour changes. People with dementia admitted to hospital are at increased risk of delirium; if unsure whether confusion is delirium or dementia, manage the delirium first.

test.q: Mary, 84, has moderate dementia. An observational pain score shows pain linked to her hip, and she is given paracetamol. What does NICE NG97 advise next?
options: Repeat the observational pain assessment after the analgesia
Record the score and repeat it at her next annual health review
Ask her to rate the pain on a 0 to 10 scale instead
Start an antipsychotic if she continues to call out
test.why: NG97 rec 1.8.5: repeat pain assessments after any pain management intervention, and when pain or behaviour change is suspected.

whyNot.1: Waiting a year misses whether the analgesia worked.
whyNot.2: Her self-report is unreliable, which is why an observational tool is used.
whyNot.3: Calling out may be ongoing pain; an antipsychotic is not the next step.
